Key steps include:\n\n* **Setup a robust project:** Initialize with React, TypeScript, Rollup (for bundling), Jest/RTL (for testing), and Storybook (for development/documentation).\n* **Structure for scalability:** Organize components, hooks, styles, and utilities for easy maintenance and growth.\n* **Build \u0026 Test Components:** Develop individual UI components (e.g., a Button example provided), write comprehensive unit tests, and create interactive Storybook stories for documentation.\n* **Publish \u0026 Version:** Configure your &#96;package.json&#96; correctly and use npm (or a private registry) to publish your versioned library effectively.\n* **Consider Advanced Topics:** Implement accessibility (A11y), theming strategies, performance optimizations, and helpful utility hooks to create a production-ready, professional-grade library.\n\n**Table of Contents** \n* 1\\. Introduction: Why Build a Component Library?\n\nAs an engineer, you understand the value of DRY (Don't Repeat Yourself) principles and maintainable code. A **React component library** embodies these by providing a centralized, versioned collection of reusable UI elements. For internal tools, this means:\n\n* **Consistency:** Ensuring all internal applications share a cohesive look, feel, and behavior.\n* **Efficiency:** Accelerating development by providing pre-built, tested UI building blocks.\n* **Maintainability:** Simplifying updates and bug fixes—change a component in the library, and it updates across all consuming applications (with version control).\n* **Quality:** Enforcing best practices, accessibility standards, and thorough testing at the component level.\n\nThis guide focuses on the technical execution of building such a library. For a higher-level overview on planning and strategy, refer to resources aimed at engineering management.\n\n## 2\\. Core Project Setup \u0026 Essential Tooling\n\nSetting up your project correctly is crucial. We'll use TypeScript for type safety, Rollup for efficient bundling, Jest for testing, and Storybook for component development and documentation.\n\nStart by initializing a new npm package and installing essential development dependencies:\n\nCopy&#96;mkdir my-react-ui-library \u0026\u0026 cd my-react-ui-library\nnpm init -y\n# Core React and build tools\nnpm install --save-dev react react-dom typescript rollup @rollup/plugin-node-resolve @rollup/plugin-commonjs @rollup/plugin-typescript @babel/preset-react @babel/preset-typescript tslib\n# Testing tools\nnpm install --save-dev jest @testing-library/react @testing-library/jest-dom jest-environment-jsdom babel-jest\n# Storybook\nnpm install --save-dev storybook @storybook/react-webpack5 @storybook/addon-essentials @storybook/addon-interactions @storybook/testing-library webpack\n# Optional: for CSS handling in Rollup\nnpm install --save-dev rollup-plugin-postcss postcss&#96;\n\n**Configure &#96;tsconfig.json&#96;** for TypeScript compilation:\n\nCopy&#96;{\n  \"compilerOptions\": {\n    \"target\": \"ES6\",            // Target modern JavaScript\n    \"module\": \"ESNext\",         // .d.ts files\n    \"declarationDir\": \"dist/types\", // Output directory for .d.ts files\n    \"outDir\": \"dist\",           // Output directory for JS files (if not using Rollup for this)\n    \"rootDir\": \"src\",           // Source directory\n    \"strict\": true,             // Enable all strict type-checking options\n    \"esModuleInterop\": true,    // Enables emit interoperability &#96;tsc&#96; is used for generating declaration files. Adjust if your setup differs.\n\n**Configure Babel (&#96;babel.config.js&#96;)** for Jest and Storybook (Rollup can use its own TypeScript plugin):\n\nCopy&#96;module.exports = {\n  presets: [\n    '@babel/preset-env', // For transpiling ES6+ down to ES5 if needed for older environments\n    '@babel/preset-react',\n    '@babel/preset-typescript',\n  ],\n};&#96;\n\n**Configure Rollup (&#96;rollup.config.js&#96;)** for bundling your library:\n\nCopy&#96;import resolve from '@rollup/plugin-node-resolve';\nimport commonjs from '@rollup/plugin-commonjs';\nimport typescript from '@rollup/plugin-typescript';\nimport postcss from 'rollup-plugin-postcss'; // If handling CSS\n// import { terser } from 'rollup-plugin-terser'; // For minification\n\nconst packageJson = require('./package.json');\n\nexport default {\n  input: 'src/index.ts', // Your library's entry point\n  output: [\n    {\n      file: packageJson.main,\n      format: 'cjs', // CommonJS for Node compatibility\n      sourcemap: true,\n    },\n    {\n      file: packageJson.module,\n      format: 'esm', // ES Module for tree shaking\n      sourcemap: true,\n    },\n  ],\n  plugins: [\n    resolve(),\n    commonjs(),\n    typescript({ tsconfig: './tsconfig.json', exclude: [\"**/*.test.tsx\", \"**/*.stories.tsx\"] }),\n    postcss({ // Example for handling CSS files\n      extract: 'styles.css', // Extracts CSS to a single file\n      minimize: true,\n    }),\n    // terser(), // Uncomment for production builds to minify\n  ],\n  external: ['react', 'react-dom'], // Externalize peer dependencies\n};&#96;\n\nEnsure your &#96;package.json&#96; has &#96;main&#96;, &#96;module&#96;, and &#96;types&#96; fields pointing to the Rollup outputs and declaration files respectively (see Publishing section).\n\n## 3\\. Structuring Your Library for Maintainability\n\nA clear folder structure is vital for a growing component library:\n\nCopy&#96;my-react-ui-library/\n├── dist/                     // Bundled output\n├── src/\n│   ├── index.ts              // Main export file for all public components/hooks\n│   ├── components/           // Directory for individual UI components\n│   │   └── Button/\n│   │       ├── Button.tsx    // Component logic and JSX\n│   │       ├── Button.module.css // Component-specific styles (CSS Modules example)\n│   │       ├── Button.stories.tsx // Storybook stories\n│   │       └── Button.test.tsx    // Jest/RTL tests\n│   │   └── AnotherComponent/\n│   ├── hooks/                // Reusable custom React hooks\n│   │   └── useSomeLogic.ts\n│   ├── styles/               // Global styles, design tokens, base styles\n│   │   ├── _variables.css    // CSS Variables for design tokens\n│   │   └── global.css\n│   └── utils/                // Shared utility functions\n│       └── helpers.ts\n├── .storybook/               // Storybook configuration\n├── jest.config.js            // Jest configuration\n├── rollup.config.js          // Rollup configuration\n├── tsconfig.json             // TypeScript configuration\n├── babel.config.js           // Babel configuration\n└── package.json&#96;\n\nYour main entry point &#96;src/index.ts&#96; should export everything you want to make public from your library:\n\nCopy&#96;// src/index.ts\nexport * from './components/Button/Button';\n// export * from './components/AnotherComponent/AnotherComponent';\n// export * from './hooks/useSomeLogic';\n// export * from './styles/global.css'; // If you want to allow global CSS import\n&#96;\n\n## 4\\. Crafting Your First Component (Button Example)\n\nLet's create a foundational &#96;Button&#96; component.\n\n**&#96;src/components/Button/Button.tsx&#96;**:\n\nCopy&#96;&#96; import React, { ButtonHTMLAttributes } from 'react';\nimport styles from './Button.module.css'; // Using CSS Modules\n\nexport interface ButtonProps extends ButtonHTMLAttributes\u003cHTMLButtonElement\u003e {\n  variant?: 'primary' | 'secondary' | 'destructive';\n  size?: 'small' | 'medium' | 'large';\n  children: React.ReactNode; // Use children for the label or content\n}\n\nexport const Button: React.FC\u003cButtonProps\u003e = ({\n  children,\n  variant = 'primary',\n  size = 'medium',\n  className = '',\n  ...props\n}) =\u003e {\n  const modeClass = styles[variant] || styles.primary;\n  const sizeClass = styles[size] || styles.medium;\n\n  return (\n    \u003cbutton\n      type=\"button\" // Default to type=\"button\" for accessibility unless overridden\n      className={&#96;${styles.buttonBase} ${modeClass} ${sizeClass} ${className}&#96;}\n      {...props}\n    \u003e\n      {children}\n    \u003c/button\u003e\n  );\n};\n &#96;&#96;\n\n**&#96;src/components/Button/Button.module.css&#96;** (Example using CSS Modules):\n\nCopy&#96;/* src/components/Button/Button.module.css */\n.buttonBase {\n  border: none;\n  padding: 10px 20px;\n  cursor: pointer;\n  font-family: inherit;\n  border-radius: 4px;\n  transition: background-color 0.2s ease-in-out, box-shadow 0.2s ease-in-out;\n  display: inline-flex;\n  align-items: center;\n  justify-content: center;\n  text-decoration: none; /* For anchor-like buttons */\n  font-weight: 700; /* Bolder for Montserrat */\n}\n\n.buttonBase:focus-visible {\n  outline: 2px solid var(--focus-ring-color, blue); /* Define --focus-ring-color in global styles */\n  outline-offset: 2px;\n}\n\n/* Variants */\n.primary {\n  background-color: var(--button-primary-bg, #007bff);\n  color: var(--button-primary-text, white);\n}\n.primary:hover {\n  background-color: var(--button-primary-hover-bg, #0056b3);\n}\n\n.secondary {\n  background-color: var(--button-secondary-bg, #6c757d);\n  color: var(--button-secondary-text, white);\n}\n.secondary:hover {\n  background-color: var(--button-secondary-hover-bg, #545b62);\n}\n\n.destructive {\n  background-color: var(--button-destructive-bg, #dc3545);\n  color: var(--button-destructive-text, white);\n}\n.destructive:hover {\n  background-color: var(--button-destructive-hover-bg, #c82333);\n}\n\n/* Sizes */\n.small {\n  padding: 6px 12px;\n  font-size: 0.875rem;\n}\n.medium {\n  padding: 10px 20px;\n  font-size: 1rem;\n}\n.large {\n  padding: 12px 24px;\n  font-size: 1.125rem;\n}\n&#96;\n\nEnsure you define CSS variables like &#96;--button-primary-bg&#96; in your global styles (e.g., &#96;src/styles/_variables.css&#96;) for theming capabilities.\n\n## 5\\. Comprehensive Testing \u0026 Storybook Integration\n\n**Testing with Jest \u0026 React Testing Library:**\n\n**&#96;jest.config.js&#96;**:\n\nCopy&#96;module.exports = {\n  testEnvironment: 'jsdom',\n  setupFilesAfterEnv: ['\u003crootDir\u003e/jest.setup.js'], // if you have a setup file\n  moduleNameMapper: {\n    '\\\\.(css|less|scss|sass)$': 'identity-obj-proxy', // Mocks CSS Modules\n  },\n  transform: {\n    '^.+\\\\.(ts|tsx|js|jsx)$': 'babel-jest',\n  },\n};\n&#96;\n\nCreate &#96;jest.setup.js&#96; (optional, for global test setup like importing &#96;@testing-library/jest-dom&#96;):\n\nCopy&#96;// jest.setup.js\nimport '@testing-library/jest-dom';\n&#96;\n\n**&#96;src/components/Button/Button.test.tsx&#96;**:\n\nCopy&#96;import React from 'react';\nimport { render, screen, fireEvent } from '@testing-library/react';\nimport { Button } from './Button';\n\ndescribe('Button Component', () =\u003e {\n  test('renders with children', () =\u003e {\n    render(\u003cButton\u003eClick Me\u003c/Button\u003e);\n    expect(screen.getByRole('button', { name: /Click Me/i })).toBeInTheDocument();\n  });\n\n  test('applies variant and size classes correctly', () =\u003e {\n    render(\u003cButton variant=\"secondary\" size=\"large\"\u003eSubmit\u003c/Button\u003e);\n    const button = screen.getByRole('button', { name: /Submit/i });\n    // Note: Testing CSS module class names can be tricky. \n    // It's often better to test visual appearance via visual regression tests.\n    // However, you can check if base classes are applied if needed.\n    expect(button).toHaveClass('buttonBase'); // from Button.module.css, actual name might be mangled\n    // For specific variant/size classes, snapshot testing or visual testing is more robust.\n  });\n\n  test('calls onClick handler when clicked', () =\u003e {\n    const handleClick = jest.fn();\n    render(\u003cButton onClick={handleClick}\u003eTest Click\u003c/Button\u003e);\n    fireEvent.click(screen.getByText('Test Click'));\n    expect(handleClick).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(1);\n  });\n\n  test('is disabled when disabled prop is true', () =\u003e {\n    render(\u003cButton disabled\u003eDisabled Button\u003c/Button\u003e);\n    expect(screen.getByRole('button', { name: /Disabled Button/i })).toBeDisabled();\n  });\n});\n&#96;\n\n**Storybook for Development and Documentation:**\n\nInitialize Storybook in your project:\n\nCopy&#96;npx storybook@latest init&#96;\n\nFollow the prompts. It should detect your React setup.\n\n**&#96;src/components/Button/Button.stories.tsx&#96;**:\n\nCopy&#96;import React from 'react';\nimport type { Meta, StoryObj } from '@storybook/react';\nimport { Button, ButtonProps } from './Button'; // Import ButtonProps\n\nconst meta: Meta\u003cButtonProps\u003e = { // Use ButtonProps for Meta type\n  title: 'Components/Button',    // How it will appear in Storybook navigation\n  component: Button,\n  tags: ['autodocs'],            // Enables auto-generated documentation\n  argTypes: {                   // Define controls for props\n    variant: {\n      control: { type: 'select' },\n      options: ['primary', 'secondary', 'destructive'],\n      description: 'The visual style of the button',\n    },\n    size: {\n      control: { type: 'select' },\n      options: ['small', 'medium', 'large'],\n      description: 'The size of the button',\n    },\n    children: {\n      control: 'text',\n      description: 'Button label or content',\n    },\n    disabled: {\n      control: 'boolean',\n      description: 'Disables the button',\n    },\n    onClick: {\n      action: 'clicked', // Logs clicks in the Storybook actions tab\n      description: 'Optional click handler',\n    },\n  },\n  parameters: {\n    layout: 'centered', // Centers the component in the Canvas tab\n  },\n};\n\nexport default meta;\n\n// Define a \"template\" story that maps args to the component\ntype Story = StoryObj\u003cButtonProps\u003e; // Use ButtonProps for Story type\n\nexport const Primary: Story = {\n  args: {\n    variant: 'primary',\n    size: 'medium',\n    children: 'Primary Button',\n  },\n};\n\nexport const Secondary: Story = {\n  args: {\n    variant: 'secondary',\n    size: 'medium',\n    children: 'Secondary Button',\n  },\n};\n\nexport const Destructive: Story = {\n  args: {\n    variant: 'destructive',\n    size: 'medium',\n    children: 'Delete',\n  },\n};\n\nexport const LargePrimary: Story = {\n  args: {\n    variant: 'primary',\n    size: 'large',\n    children: 'Large Primary',\n  },\n};\n\nexport const SmallSecondary: Story = {\n  args: {\n    variant: 'secondary',\n    size: 'small',\n    children: 'Small Secondary',\n  },\n};\n\nexport const Disabled: Story = {\n  args: {\n    variant: 'primary',\n    children: 'Disabled Button',\n    disabled: true,\n  },\n};\n&#96;\n\nRun Storybook with &#96;npm run storybook&#96;.\n\n## 6\\. Publishing \u0026 Versioning Your Library\n\nOnce your components are ready, you'll publish your library to a package registry (like npm or a private registry).\n\n**Update &#96;package.json&#96;** with necessary fields:\n\nCopy&#96;{\n  \"name\": \"my-react-ui-library\",\n  \"version\": \"0.1.0\",\n  \"private\": false, // Set to false to publish\n  \"description\": \"A fantastic React UI component library.\",\n  \"author\": \"Your Name \u003cyouremail@example.com\u003e\",\n  \"license\": \"MIT\", // Or your chosen license\n  \"repository\": {\n    \"type\": \"git\",\n    \"url\": \"https://github.com/yourusername/my-react-ui-library.git\" // Replace\n  },\n  \"main\": \"dist/index.cjs.js\", // CommonJS entry point from Rollup\n  \"module\": \"dist/index.esm.js\", // ES Module entry point from Rollup\n  \"types\": \"dist/types/index.d.ts\", // TypeScript definitions entry point\n  \"files\": [ // Files to include in the published package\n    \"dist\"\n  ],\n  \"scripts\": {\n    \"build\": \"rollup -c\", // Your build command\n    \"test\": \"jest\",\n    \"storybook\": \"storybook dev -p 6006\",\n    \"build-storybook\": \"storybook build\",\n    \"lint\": \"eslint src --ext .ts,.tsx\",\n    \"clean\": \"rm -rf dist\" // Script to clean the dist folder\n  },\n  \"peerDependencies\": { // Specify peer dependencies\n    \"react\": \"^17.0.0 || ^18.0.0\",\n    \"react-dom\": \"^17.0.0 || ^18.0.0\"\n  },\n  \"devDependencies\": {\n    // ... your dev dependencies ...\n  },\n  \"dependencies\": {\n    // \"tslib\": \"^2.x.x\" // tslib is often a runtime dependency when using --importHelpers in tsconfig or by some TS features\n  }\n}\n&#96;\n\n**Publishing Steps:**\n\n1. Ensure your code is committed and pushed to your Git repository.\n2. Build your library: &#96;npm run build&#96; (this should run Rollup and tsc for declarations).\n3. Log in to npm (or your private registry): &#96;npm login&#96;.\n4. Update the version (semantic versioning is recommended):&#96;npm version patch&#96; (for bug fixes: 0.1.0 -\u003e 0.1.1)  \n&#96;npm version minor&#96; (for new features, non-breaking: 0.1.0 -\u003e 0.2.0)  \n&#96;npm version major&#96; (for breaking changes: 0.1.0 -\u003e 1.0.0)\n5. Publish: &#96;npm publish&#96; (add &#96;--access public&#96; if publishing a scoped package to npm for the first time).\n6. Push tags to Git: &#96;git push --tags&#96;.\n\nConsider using tools like &#96;semantic-release&#96; to automate the versioning and publishing process based on commit messages.\n\n## 7\\. Advanced Considerations for Robust Libraries\n\nAs your library grows, consider these advanced topics:\n\n* **Accessibility (A11y):**  \n   * Go beyond basic ARIA attributes. Ensure full keyboard navigability for all interactive components.  \n   * Test with screen readers (NVDA, VoiceOver, JAWS).  \n   * Manage focus states meticulously, especially for modals, dropdowns, and other overlay components.  \n   * Use tools like &#96;@axe-core/react&#96; for automated accessibility checks during development and testing.  \n   * Provide clear documentation on any accessibility implications of your components.\n* **Theming Strategies:**  \n   * **CSS Custom Properties (Variables):** Highly recommended for modern libraries. Define a set of global and component-specific CSS variables for colors, fonts, spacing, etc. Consumers can then override these variables to theme the library.  \n   * **React Context API:** For more dynamic theming or when CSS variables are insufficient (e.g., switching between light/dark mode which might involve more than just CSS). Provide a ThemeProvider component.  \n   * **Styled-components / Emotion Theming:** If using CSS-in-JS, leverage their built-in theming capabilities.  \n   * Document clearly how to apply and customize themes.\n* **Performance Optimization:**  \n   * Use &#96;React.memo&#96; for functional components and &#96;shouldComponentUpdate&#96; (or &#96;PureComponent&#96;) for class components to prevent unnecessary re-renders.  \n   * Memoize expensive calculations with &#96;useMemo&#96; and callbacks with &#96;useCallback&#96;.  \n   * Be mindful of bundle size. Analyze your bundle with tools like &#96;rollup-plugin-visualizer&#96; or &#96;webpack-bundle-analyzer&#96;.  \n   * Lazy load components or parts of your library if they are not immediately needed.  \n   * Ensure efficient event handling and avoid memory leaks.\n* **Developing Utility Hooks \u0026 Data Connectors (Helpers):**  \n   * For internal tools, you might identify common data fetching patterns or interactions with specific internal APIs/databases.  \n   * Create custom hooks (e.g., &#96;useInternalApi(endpoint, options)&#96;) that encapsulate this logic. These hooks are part of your library but are not UI components.  \n   * These hooks can handle loading states, error handling, and data transformation, making it easier for consuming applications to interact with backends consistently.  \n   Copy&#96;&#96; // Example: src/hooks/useQueryData.ts  \n   import { useState, useEffect, useCallback } from 'react';  \n   interface QueryDataOptions {  \n     // Define options: method, headers, body etc.  \n     method?: 'GET' | 'POST' | 'PUT' | 'DELETE';  \n     headers?: Record\u003cstring, string\u003e;  \n     body?: any;  \n   }  \n   export function useQueryData\u003cT\u003e(url: string, options?: QueryDataOptions) {  \n     const [data, setData] = useState\u003cT | null\u003e(null);  \n     const [loading, setLoading] = useState(true);  \n     const [error, setError] = useState\u003cError | null\u003e(null);  \n     const fetchData = useCallback(async () =\u003e {  \n       setLoading(true);  \n       setError(null);  \n       try {  \n         const fetchOptions = {  \n           method: options?.method || 'GET',  \n           headers: {  \n             'Content-Type': 'application/json',  \n             ...options?.headers,  \n           },  \n           body: options?.body ? JSON.stringify(options.body) : undefined,  \n         };  \n         // Replace with your actual fetch logic, error handling, auth etc.  \n         const response = await fetch(url, fetchOptions);  \n         if (!response.ok) {  \n           throw new Error(&#96;HTTP error! status: ${response.status}&#96;);  \n         }  \n         const result = await response.json();  \n         setData(result);  \n       } catch (e) {  \n         setError(e as Error);  \n       } finally {  \n         setLoading(false);  \n       }  \n     }, [url, options]); // Consider options dependency carefully if it's not stable  \n     useEffect(() =\u003e {  \n       fetchData();  \n     }, [fetchData]); // Re-run if fetchData changes (due to url/options change)  \n     return { data, loading, error, refetch: fetchData };  \n   }  \n    &#96;&#96;\n* **Contribution Guidelines \u0026 Code Review:**  \n   * If multiple engineers contribute, establish clear guidelines: coding style (use Prettier and ESLint), commit message conventions, branching strategy (e.g., Gitflow), and PR process.  \n   * Enforce code reviews to maintain quality, share knowledge, and ensure consistency.  \n   * Automate checks with linters and formatters in your CI pipeline.\n* **Internationalization (i18n) and Localization (l10n):**  \n   * If your internal tools need to support multiple languages, plan for i18n from the start. This might involve passing locale props or using a context-based i18n library.\n* **Visual Regression Testing:**  \n   * Tools like Chromatic (by Storybook maintainers), Percy, or Applitools can help catch unintended visual changes in your components.\n\n## 8\\. Conclusion \u0026 Best Practices\n\nBuilding a high-quality **React component library** is an iterative process that requires careful planning, robust tooling, and a commitment to best practices. As an engineer, your focus should be on:\n\n* **Component Design:** Create flexible, composable, and accessible components with clear APIs.\n* **Code Quality:** Write clean, maintainable, and well-typed TypeScript code.\n* **Thorough Testing:** Implement comprehensive unit, integration, and potentially visual regression tests.\n* **Excellent Documentation:** Use Storybook effectively to provide interactive examples and clear usage guidelines. Engineers are key contributors to good documentation.\n* **Collaboration:** If working in a team, follow established contribution guidelines and participate actively in code reviews.\n* **Continuous Improvement:** Regularly revisit and refactor components, optimize for performance, and incorporate feedback from users of the library.\n\nA well-crafted component library will significantly improve the efficiency, consistency, and quality of your organization's internal tools, making it a valuable asset for the engineering team.\n\nDinesh Kumar, VP Engineering, Yubi Group \n\n### \"We didnt build our library for internal tools; we rather used DronaHQ low code platform!\"\n\n \"Building and maintaining our own React component library was a huge time sink. We switched to **DronaHQ**, a visual dev tool, and it's made building internal tools **10x simpler and faster** for our entire engineering team. Now we focus on solving business problems, not UI plumbing.\"\n\n Dinesh Kumar\n\n VP Engineering, Yubi Group\n\n Simplify Your Internal Tooling → ",

      "chunk": "James IvesHome\n* Home\n* About\n* Blog\n* Projects\n\n# Documenting Web Components With Storybook\n\nPublished 5 months ago\n\n17 min read\n\n12,456 views \n\n## Overview\n\nDocumentation is a crucial part of any design system. There's the aspect of writing, maintaining, and ensuring that it doesn't drift from the codebase. It's a lot of work, and it's easy to let it slip. I've spent a lot of time over the last year and a half thinking about the right way to document components, and it took some time until I found a sustainable solution I was happy with. In this article, I want to discuss how you can easily document your Web Components with Storybook so that your documentation provides a good user and developer experience.\n\nStorybook\n\nOnce upon a time...\n\n## Custom Elements Manifest\n\nOne of the best tools available in Web Component development is the Custom Elements Manifest. It's a JSON representation of all your available components, covering all the attributes, methods, slots and events they support, powered by your JSDoc comments and TypeScript types. You can customize the manifest generation through plugins to support custom JSDoc comments, allowing you to power more pieces of your documentation through code comments; for example, you could set up a comment format to indicate if your component is experimental or stable or provide a way to add a link to your Figma files.\n\nsrc/components/sb-button/sb-button.ts\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;js\nimport { LitElement, css, html } from \"lit\";\nimport { customElement, property } from \"lit/decorators.js\";\n\n/**\n * The Button component, used for calling attention to actions.\n *\n * @customElement sb-button\n * @github https://github.com/starbucks/web-components\n * @figma https://figma.com\n *\n * @slot - The main content area of the button.\n * @csspart button - Allows you to style the button element.\n */\n@customElement(\"sb-button\")\nexport default class SBButton extends LitElement {\n  /**\n   * Determines the variant of the button.\n   */\n  @property({ type: String })\n  public variant: \"primary\" | \"secondary\" = \"primary\";\n\n  /**\n   * Disables the button.\n   */\n  @property({ type: Boolean })\n  public disabled?: boolean;\n\n  /**\n   * @inheritdoc\n   */\n  public render() {\n    return html&#96;\n      \u003ca\n        part=\"button\"\n        ?disabled=${this.disabled}\n        class=\"${this.variant === \"primary\" ? \"primary\" : \"secondary\"}\"\n      \u003e\n        \u003cspan\u003e\u003cslot\u003e\u003c/slot\u003e \u003c/span\u003e\n      \u003c/a\u003e\n    &#96;;\n  }\n\n  static styles = css&#96;&#96;;\n}\n\ndeclare global {\n  interface HTMLElementTagNameMap {\n    \"sb-button\": SBButton;\n  }\n}\n\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nMy favourite Custom Elements Manifest generator is the one by open-wc. The setup is straightforward: you create a config file and tell it where to find your components. It even has support for Lit out of the box.\n\ncustom-elements-manifest.config.js\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;js\nimport { jsDocTagsPlugin } from \"@wc-toolkit/jsdoc-tags\";\n\nexport default {\n  globs: [\"src/components/**/*.ts\"],\n  outdir: \"public\",\n  litelement: true,\n  dev: false,\n  plugins: [\n    jsDocTagsPlugin({\n      tags: {\n        figma: {\n          description: \"Link to the Figma design\",\n          type: \"string\",\n          tagMapping: \"figma\",\n        },\n        github: {\n          description: \"Link to the GitHub repo\",\n          type: \"string\",\n          tagMapping: \"github\",\n        },\n      },\n    }),\n  ],\n};\n\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nAfter you've generated the Custom Elements Manifest, you'll see how vast the dataset is. You're creating a payload that lets you query all the intricate details about your components, which is ideal for automatically generating documentation.\n\npublic/custom-elements.json\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;json\n{\n  \"schemaVersion\": \"1.0.0\",\n  \"readme\": \"\",\n  \"modules\": [\n    {\n      \"kind\": \"javascript-module\",\n      \"path\": \"src/components/sb-button/sb-button.stories.ts\",\n      \"declarations\": [\n        {\n          \"kind\": \"variable\",\n          \"name\": \"meta\",\n          \"type\": {\n            \"text\": \"Meta\u003cSBButton\u003e\"\n          },\n          \"default\": \"{ title: \\\"Components/Button\\\", component, args, argTypes, parameters: { actions: { handles: events, }, }, render: (args) =\u003e template(args), }\"\n        },\n        {\n          \"kind\": \"variable\",\n          \"name\": \"Secondary\",\n          \"type\": {\n            \"text\": \"Story\"\n          },\n          \"default\": \"{ args: { \\\"default-slot\\\": \\\"Secondary Button\\\", variant: \\\"secondary\\\", }, }\"\n        },\n        {\n          \"kind\": \"variable\",\n          \"name\": \"Primary\",\n          \"type\": {\n            \"text\": \"Story\"\n          },\n          \"default\": \"{ args: { \\\"default-slot\\\": \\\"Primary Button\\\", variant: \\\"primary\\\", }, }\"\n        }\n      ],\n      \"exports\": [\n        {\n          \"kind\": \"js\",\n          \"name\": \"default\",\n          \"declaration\": {\n            \"name\": \"meta\",\n            \"module\": \"src/components/sb-button/sb-button.stories.ts\"\n          }\n        },\n        {\n          \"kind\": \"js\",\n          \"name\": \"Secondary\",\n          \"declaration\": {\n            \"name\": \"Secondary\",\n            \"module\": \"src/components/sb-button/sb-button.stories.ts\"\n          }\n        },\n        {\n          \"kind\": \"js\",\n          \"name\": \"sb-card\",\n          \"declaration\": {\n            \"name\": \"SBCard\",\n            \"module\": \"src/components/sb-card/sb-card.ts\"\n          }\n        }\n      ]\n    }\n  ]\n}\n\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nSo many good plugins for the generator allow you to enhance the developer experience for those using your components. For instance, you can enable VSCode IDE highlighting on your custom elements using the custom-element-vs-code-integration plugin and generate TypeScript mappings for those using your components in JSX with custom-element-jsx-integration. Getting the most out of the Custom Elements Manifest depends on how well you comment and type your codebase, which we should all strive to improve anyway.\n\n## Wiring the Controls\n\nStorybook Controls is one of the best features of Storybook, but it's also one I've seen teams struggle with the most. If you've wired up your story to include all of the available parameters, it will build an interface that allows your users to toggle things on and off to see how the component reacts in real time. This feature is super helpful as it will enable your users to understand your component API better and how things work before they implement it in their application. It also helps QA teams test your components more effectively.\n\nStorybook Controls\n\nExample of Storybook Controls\n\nThe problem, however, is that this is quite cumbersome to maintain. If you do this manually, you'll end up where things are often broken or left out of the table unless you have exceptional discipline. Most of the feedback I've gotten from teams struggling with Storybook is that this is their biggest pain point; however, using the Custom Elements Manifest file we generated, there's a better way, as it already knows everything about our components.\n\nsrc/components/sb-button/sb-button.stories.ts\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;ts\nconst meta: Meta\u003cSBButton\u003e = {\n  title: \"Components/Button\",\n  component,\n  argTypes: {\n    variant: {\n      options: [\"primary\", \"secondary\"],\n      control: { type: \"radio\" },\n    },\n  },\n  render: (args) =\u003e html&#96;\u003csb-button .variant=${args.variant}\u003e\u003c/sb-button\u003e&#96;,\n};\n\nexport default meta;\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nImagining having to maintain the argTypes object for EVERY parameter?\n\nWiring up your stories to read from the Custom Elements Manifest is a matter of creating a function that parses it, outputs the correct schema Storybook expects, and then spreads any attributes directly onto your component. We'll need to provide the methods with the associated element name at a minimum so it knows what to key off of. I've put together a small example of what this _could_ look like.\n\n.storybook/controls.ts\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;ts\nfunction getArgTypesFromManifest(manifest: Manifest, componentName: string) {\n  const module = manifest.modules.find((mod) =\u003e\n    mod.declarations.some((decl) =\u003e decl.tagName === componentName)\n  );\n\n  if (!module) return {};\n\n  const declaration = module.declarations.find(\n    (decl) =\u003e decl.tagName === componentName\n  );\n\n  if (!declaration) return {};\n\n  const argTypes: Record\u003cstring, ArgType\u003e = {};\n\n  declaration.attributes.forEach((attr) =\u003e {\n    argTypes[attr.name] = {\n      control: { type: getControlType(attr.type.text) },\n      description: attr.description,\n      defaultValue: attr.default,\n      options: getOptions(attr.type.text),\n    };\n  });\n\n  return { argTypes };\n}\n\nfunction getControlType(type: string): string {\n  if (type.includes(\"|\")) {\n    return \"select\";\n  }\n  switch (type) {\n    case \"string\":\n      return \"text\";\n    case \"number\":\n      return \"number\";\n    case \"boolean\":\n      return \"boolean\";\n    default:\n      return \"text\";\n  }\n}\n\nfunction getOptions(type: string): string[] {\n  if (type.includes(\"|\")) {\n    return type.split(\"|\").map((option) =\u003e option.trim().replace(/\"/g, \"\"));\n  }\n  return [];\n}\n\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nMaintaining this code yourself can be challenging as there's a lot of nuance in how things are defined in the manifest file. Instead of writing this yourself, I recommend using this excellent plugin from Burton Smith, which handles this piece for you. Using this plugin, you can manipulate CSS variables, slots and other things directly from Storybook controls with minimal boilerplate. It's fantastic, and everyone should use it; seriously, don't write this yourself; it's much better with the plugin.\n\n/src/components/sb-button/sb-button.stories.ts\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;ts\nimport type { Meta, StoryObj } from \"@storybook/web-components\";\nimport SBButton from \"./sb-button\";\nimport { getWcStorybookHelpers } from \"wc-storybook-helpers\";\nimport \"./sb-button\";\n\nconst component = \"sb-button\";\nconst { events, args, argTypes, template } = getWcStorybookHelpers(component);\ntype Story = StoryObj\u003cSBButton \u0026 typeof args\u003e;\n\nconst meta: Meta\u003cSBButton\u003e = {\n  title: \"Components/Button\",\n  component,\n  args,\n  argTypes,\n  parameters: {\n    actions: {\n      handles: events,\n    },\n  },\n  render: (args) =\u003e template(args),\n};\nexport default meta;\n\nexport const Primary: Story = {\n  args: {\n    \"default-slot\": \"Primary Button\",\n  },\n};\n\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nMuch better.\n\nWith your controls automatically generating, you can now focus on writing high-quality code and comments without worrying about Storybook.\n\nTo reduce any setup fatigue, I add a \\*.stories.ts file alongside my component generator, which sets up everything the plugin needs to start automating Storybook Controls from day 0.\n\n## Docs\n\nWhen it comes to documentation, you must understand your audience. That's not just those viewing your documentation but also those writing it. While having a fancy documentation site is excellent, maintaining one takes a lot of work. It's also not easy to break habits; if most of your users are visiting your Storybook already, they'll likely continue to do so even after you launch your new site, so wouldn't it be better to meet them where they are? If you don't have specific requirements, Storybook Docs will likely suffice as the vessel for your documentation for your designers and engineers. Your engineers can continue to have their documentation automatically generated while your designers and product owners can contribute with markdown.\n\nMy approach to documenting in Storybook is to have a template that applies to everything by default, with a simple way to provide manually injected content where it makes sense. To do this, I first set up a documentation template; setting up a template can be done by extending your Storybook configuration and pointing it towards a markdown file.\n\n.storybook/preview.ts\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;ts\nimport type { Preview } from \"@storybook/web-components\";\nimport { setCustomElementsManifest } from \"@storybook/web-components\";\nimport customElements from \"./custom-elements.json\";\nimport DocumentationTemplate from \"./DocumentationTemplate.mdx\";\n\nsetCustomElementsManifest(customElements);\n\nconst preview: Preview = {\n  tags: [\"autodocs\"],\n  parameters: {\n    docs: {\n      template: DocumentationTemplate,\n    },\n    controls: {\n      expanded: true,\n      matchers: {\n        color: /(background|color)$/i,\n        date: /Date$/i,\n      },\n    },\n  },\n};\n\nexport default preview;\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nOut of the box, Storybook has several documentation-orientated components you can use, which they call blocks. You use them to display things like the component title, description, and the controls we created earlier.\n\n.storybook/DocumentationTemplate.mdx\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;markdown\nimport { Meta, Title, Primary, Controls, Stories } from '@storybook/blocks';\n \n \n\u003cMeta isTemplate /\u003e\n \n\u003cTitle /\u003e\n \n# Default implementation\n \n\u003cPrimary /\u003e\n \n## Inputs\n \nThe component accepts the following inputs (props):\n \n\u003cControls /\u003e\n \n---\n \n## Additional variations\n \nListed below are additional variations of the component.\n \n\u003cStories /\u003e\n\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nMany of these out-of-the-box components, however, don't fit the bill. We want our Custom Elements Manifest to drive our documentation; it's no good if we define a bunch of custom JSDoc comments if they aren't used in our documentation, right? Fortunately, Storybook provides a way to define your own custom blocks using the &#96;of&#96; hook. Using this hook, we can tap into the metadata provided by our story to get the component name; we can then fetch the Custom Elements Manifest JSON file and pull data directly from it into our documentation. We can use this technique to set up instructions on installing our component or a list of badges based on what the component supports. More importantly, you can use your own design system elements to make everything look ✨ official ✨.\n\n.storybook/blocks/Install.jsx\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;jsx\nimport { useOf, Markdown } from '@storybook/blocks';\nimport React from 'react';\n\n/**\n * Renders an install block for a component.\n */\nconst Install = ({ of }) =\u003e {\n  const resolvedOf = useOf(of || 'story', ['story', 'meta']);\n  let componentName = '';\n\n  switch (resolvedOf.type) {\n    case 'story': {\n      componentName = resolvedOf.story.component\n      break;\n    }\n    default: {\n      componentName = '';\n    }\n  }\n\n  const markdown = &#96;\\&#96;\\&#96;\\&#96;javascript\n      npm install @starbucks/${componentName.toLowerCase().replace(/\\s+/g, '-')}\n    \\&#96;\\&#96;\\&#96;&#96;;\n\n  return \u003cMarkdown\u003e{markdown}\u003c/Markdown\u003e;\n};\n\nexport default Install\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\n.storybook/blocks/Title.jsx\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;jsx\nimport React, { useEffect, useState } from 'react';\nimport { Title as BlocksTitle, useOf } from '@storybook/blocks';\nimport { GitHubLogo, FigmaLogo } from './Logos';\n\n/**\n * Renders a title block for a component, including any associated GitHub and Figma links.\n */\nconst Title = ({ of }) =\u003e {\n  const [componentName, setComponentName] = useState('');\n  const [githubLink, setGithubLink] = useState('');\n  const [figmaLink, setFigmaLink] = useState('');\n\n  const resolvedOf = useOf(of || 'story', ['story', 'meta']);\n\n  useEffect(() =\u003e {\n    const fetchComponentData = async () =\u003e {\n      let componentName = '';\n\n      switch (resolvedOf.type) {\n        case 'story': {\n          componentName = resolvedOf.story.component;\n          break;\n        }\n        default: {\n          componentName = '';\n        }\n      }\n\n      setComponentName(componentName);\n\n      try {\n        const response = await fetch('/public/custom-elements.json');\n        const manifest = await response.json();\n        const component = manifest.modules.find(module =\u003e module.declarations.some(declaration =\u003e declaration.tagName === componentName));\n        if (component) {\n          const declaration = component.declarations.find(declaration =\u003e declaration.tagName === componentName);\n          if (declaration.github) {\n            setGithubLink(declaration.github.name);\n          }\n          if (declaration.figma) {\n            setFigmaLink(declaration.figma.name);\n          }\n        }\n      } catch (error) {\n        console.error('Error fetching JSON:', error);\n      }\n    };\n\n    fetchComponentData();\n  }, [resolvedOf]);\n\n  return (\n    \u003cdiv style={{ display: 'flex', justifyContent: 'space-between', alignItems: 'center' }}\u003e\n      \u003cBlocksTitle /\u003e\n      \u003cdiv style={{ display: 'flex', gap: '10px' }}\u003e\n        {githubLink \u0026\u0026 (\n          \u003ca href={githubLink} target=\"_blank\" rel=\"noopener noreferrer\"\u003e\n            \u003cGitHubLogo /\u003e\n          \u003c/a\u003e\n        )}\n        {figmaLink \u0026\u0026 (\n          \u003ca href={figmaLink} target=\"_blank\" rel=\"noopener noreferrer\"\u003e\n            \u003cFigmaLogo /\u003e\n          \u003c/a\u003e\n        )}\n      \u003c/div\u003e\n    \u003c/div\u003e\n  );\n};\n\nexport default Title;\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nYou can then update your default documentation template to reference these components.\n\n.storybook/DocumentationTemplate.mdx\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;md\nimport { Meta, Description,  Primary, Controls, Stories } from '@storybook/blocks';\nimport Install from './blocks/Install';\nimport Title from './blocks/Title';\n \n \n\u003cMeta isTemplate /\u003e\n \n\u003cTitle /\u003e\n\u003cDescription /\u003e\n\u003cInstall /\u003e\n\n\u003cPrimary /\u003e\n\n## Inputs\n\nThe component accepts the following inputs (props):\n\n\u003cControls /\u003e\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nWith this setup, you can now automatically generate documentation that is consistent and up-to-date with your codebase.\n\nStorybook Docs\n\nFully automatic.\n\nSimilarly, you can use these same components in your own manually create",

to Facebook  Share to Mastodon \n\nShare Post via... Report Abuse \n\nCover image for A Guide to Storybook: UI Development, Testing, and Documentation \n\nAustin Welsh \n\nAustin Welsh \n\n Posted on Feb 17 \n\n#  A Guide to Storybook: UI Development, Testing, and Documentation\n\n#webdev #ui #react #javascript \n\n👋 **Let's Connect!** Follow me on GitHub for new projects.\n\n---\n\n## **Introduction** \n\nBuilding **consistent and scalable UI components** is crucial in modern web development. **Storybook** is a tool that allows developers to **isolate, develop, test, and document UI components** in a sandboxed environment. \n\nStorybook enables you to:  \n  \n✅ **Develop components in isolation** without running a full application.  \n  \n✅ **Create a component library** for design consistency.  \n  \n✅ **Test and document UI behavior** interactively.  \n  \n✅ **Integrate with frameworks like React, Vue, Angular, and more**. \n\nIn this comprehensive guide, we’ll cover: \n\n* **Setting up Storybook**\n* **Writing and organizing stories**\n* **Using add-ons and controls**\n* **Testing components with Storybook**\n* **Mocking API requests**\n* **Visual regression testing**\n* **Automating accessibility testing**\n* **Snapshot testing**\n* **Theming in Storybook**\n* **Integrating Storybook with Playwright for E2E testing**\n* **Deploying Storybook as documentation**\n* **Best practices for Storybook projects**\n\n---\n\n##  What is Storybook?\n\nStorybook is an open-source tool for **building UI components in isolation**. It provides a dedicated environment for testing and documenting components **without running the entire application**. \n\n### **Why Use Storybook?** \n\n| Feature                                                | Storybook |\n| ------------------------------------------------------ | --------- |\n| Develop components **in isolation**                    | ✅ Yes     |\n| Interactive **component preview**                      | ✅ Yes     |\n| Built-in **documentation generation**                  | ✅ Yes     |\n| Supports **multiple frameworks** (React, Vue, Angular) | ✅ Yes     |\n| Integration with **Jest, Testing Library, Playwright** | ✅ Yes     |\n\n---\n\n##  Installing and Setting Up Storybook\n\nStorybook can be installed in a new or existing project. \n\n### **Installation for React** \n\nRun the following command in your project directory:  \n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\nnpx storybook@latest init\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nEnter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode \n\n✔ Automatically detects the framework and **configures Storybook**.  \n  \n✔ Generates a &#96;.storybook&#96; folder with configuration files.  \n  \n✔ Creates example stories to get started. \n\n### **Starting Storybook** \n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\nnpm run storybook\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nEnter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode \n\nStorybook will launch on &#96;http://localhost:6006/&#96;.\n\n---\n\n##  Writing Your First Story\n\nA **story** represents a UI component's **state**. It defines how the component should appear in different scenarios. \n\n### **Basic Button Story (React Example)** \n\nCreate a file **&#96;Button.stories.js&#96;** inside &#96;src/components/Button/&#96;.  \n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\nimport React from 'react';\nimport Button from './Button';\n\nexport default {\n  title: 'Components/Button',\n  component: Button,\n};\n\nexport const Primary = () =\u003e \u003cButton label=\"Primary Button\" /\u003e;\nexport const Secondary = () =\u003e \u003cButton label=\"Secondary Button\" variant=\"secondary\" /\u003e;\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nEnter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode \n\n✔ Each **export** represents a different **state of the component**.  \n  \n✔ &#96;title&#96; defines the **category in Storybook**.  \n  \n✔ &#96;component&#96; links the **UI component** to the story. \n\n---\n\n##  Using Controls for Dynamic Interaction\n\nStorybook Controls allow developers to modify props dynamically in the UI.\n\n###  Example: Adding Controls to Button\n\nModify &#96;Button.stories.js&#96;:  \n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\nexport const Playground = (args) =\u003e \u003cButton {...args} /\u003e;\n\nPlayground.args = {\n  label: 'Dynamic Button',\n  variant: 'primary',\n};\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nEnter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode \n\nNow, Storybook will provide a UI panel where developers can change **label** and **variant** dynamically.\n\n✔ Helps **test different states** without modifying the code.\n\n---\n\n##  Enhancing Storybook with Add-ons\n\nStorybook Add-ons extend functionality.\n\n###  Popular Storybook Add-ons\n\n| Add-on                     | Purpose                  |\n| -------------------------- | ------------------------ |\n| @storybook/addon-controls  | Adjust props dynamically |\n| @storybook/addon-docs      | Generate documentation   |\n| @storybook/addon-a11y      | Accessibility testing    |\n| @storybook/testing-library | UI interaction testing   |\n\n###  Installing an Add-on\n\nExample: Installing the **Accessibility Add-on**  \n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\nnpm install @storybook/addon-a11y --save-dev\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nEnter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode \n\nModify &#96;.storybook/main.js&#96; to **register the add-on**:  \n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\nmodule.exports = {\n  addons: ['@storybook/addon-a11y'],\n};\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nEnter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode \n\n✔ Adds an \"Accessibility\" panel to test contrast, ARIA attributes, and color issues.\n\n---\n\n##  Organizing Stories for Scalability\n\nA well-structured Storybook project improves maintainability. \n\n### **Recommended Folder Structure** \n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n📂 src\n ┣ 📂 components\n ┃ ┣ 📂 Button\n ┃ ┃ ┣ 📜 Button.js\n ┃ ┃ ┣ 📜 Button.stories.js\n ┃ ┃ ┣ 📜 Button.test.js\n ┣ 📂 .storybook\n ┃ ┣ 📜 main.js   # Configurations\n ┃ ┣ 📜 preview.js  # Global decorators\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nEnter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode \n\n✔ Each component has **its own folder** for easy organization.  \n  \n✔ &#96;.storybook/main.js&#96; manages **configurations** and **add-ons**. \n\n---\n\n##  Automating Accessibility Testing in Storybook\n\nEnsuring your UI components are **accessible** is crucial for usability. Storybook integrates with **accessibility testing tools** to automatically detect potential issues.\n\n### **Installing the Accessibility Add-on** \n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\nnpm install --save-dev @storybook/addon-a11y\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nEnter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode \n\n### **Enabling the Add-on** \n\nModify &#96;.storybook/main.js&#96;:  \n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\nmodule.exports = {\n  addons: ['@storybook/addon-a11y'],\n};\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nEnter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode \n\n### **Running Accessibility Tests** \n\nWhen the Storybook UI loads, a new **\"Accessibility\" panel** appears, displaying any detected issues.\n\n✔ Automatically **checks for contrast issues, missing ARIA attributes, and keyboard accessibility**.  \n  \n✔ Helps fix **WCAG compliance issues** before production. \n\n---\n\n##  Visual Regression Testing in Storybook\n\n**Visual Regression Testing** detects UI changes by comparing rendered components **before and after updates**. This ensures that UI modifications do not introduce **unintended design changes**.\n\n### **Installing Visual Testing Add-ons** \n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\nnpm install --save-dev @storybook/addon-visual-tests\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nEnter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode \n\n### **Adding a Screenshot Test** \n\nModify &#96;Button.stories.js&#96;:  \n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\nimport { within, userEvent } from '@storybook/testing-library';\n\nexport const VisualTest = () =\u003e \u003cButton label=\"Click me\" /\u003e;\n\nVisualTest.play = async ({ canvasElement }) =\u003e {\n  const canvas = within(canvasElement);\n  const button = canvas.getByRole('button');\n  await userEvent.click(button);\n};\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nEnter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode \n\n### **Running Visual Tests** \n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\nnpx storybook test\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nEnter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode \n\n✔ Detects UI changes with **automatic snapshot comparisons**. \n\n---\n\n##  Mocking API Calls in Storybook\n\nStorybook can mock API requests to test UI behavior without relying on a backend.\n\n###  Example: Mocking an API Response\n\nInstall Mock Service Worker (MSW):  \n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\nnpm install msw --save-dev\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nEnter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode \n\nCreate &#96;mocks.js&#96;:  \n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\nimport { setupWorker, rest } from 'msw';\n\nexport const worker = setupWorker(\n  rest.get('/api/user', (req, res, ctx) =\u003e {\n    return res(ctx.json({ name: 'Mock User' }));\n  })\n);\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nEnter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode \n\nStart the mock server in &#96;preview.js&#96;:  \n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\nimport { worker } from '../mocks';\n\nworker.start();\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nEnter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode \n\n✔ Components now receive mock API responses during development.\n\n---\n\n##  Integrating Storybook with Playwright for E2E Testing\n\nStorybook can be used with **Playwright** to perform **end-to-end (E2E) testing** for UI components.\n\n### **Installing Playwright** \n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\nnpm install --save-dev @playwright/test\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nEnter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode \n\n### **Writing a Playwright Test for a Storybook Component** \n\nCreate a file &#96;Button.spec.js&#96;:  \n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\nconst { test, expect } = require('@playwright/test');\n\ntest('Check if Button component renders', async ({ page }) =\u003e {\n    await page.goto('http://localhost:6006/?path=/story/components-button--primary');\n    const button = await page.locator('button');\n    await expect(button).toHaveText('Primary Button');\n});\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nEnter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode \n\n### **Running the Playwright Test** \n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\nnpx playwright test\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nEnter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode \n\n✔ **Combines UI component testing with full browser automation**. \n\n---\n\n##  Writing Component Tests in Storybook\n\nStorybook integrates with Jest, Testing Library, and Playwright for UI testing.\n\n###  Example: Testing with Jest + Testing Library\n\nInstall dependencies:  \n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\nnpm install @testing-library/react jest --save-dev\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nEnter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode \n\nCreate &#96;Button.test.js&#96;:  \n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\nimport { render, screen } from '@testing-library/react';\nimport Button from './Button';\n\ntest('renders the button', () =\u003e {\n  render(\u003cButton label=\"Click Me\" /\u003e);\n  expect(screen.getByText('Click Me')).toBeInTheDocument();\n});\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nEnter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode \n\n✔ Ensures components render correctly.  \n✔ Runs with npm test.\n\n---\n\n##  Deploying Storybook as Documentation\n\nStorybook can be deployed as a **component documentation site**.\n\n### **Generate Static Build** \n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\nnpm run build-storybook\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nEnter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode \n\nThis creates a **&#96;storybook-static/&#96;** folder.\n\n### **Deploy to GitHub Pages** \n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\nnpx storybook-to-ghpages\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nEnter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode \n\n✔ Makes Storybook accessible via **GitHub Pages or any static host**. \n\n---\n\n##  Running Storybook in CI/CD\n\nIntegrating Storybook in CI/CD pipelines ensures UI consistency across development.\n\n###  GitHub Actions Example\n\nCreate &#96;.github/workflows/storybook.yml&#96;:  \n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\nname: Storybook CI\non: push\njobs:\n  test:\n    runs-on: ubuntu-latest\n    steps:\n      - name: Checkout Code\n        uses: actions/checkout@v2\n      - name: Install Dependencies\n        run: npm install\n      - name: Build Storybook\n        run: npm run build-storybook\n      - name: Deploy Storybook\n        run: npx storybook-to-ghpages\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nEnter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode \n\n✔ Runs Storybook on every code push.\n\n---\n\n##  Best Practices for Storybook Projects\n\n✔ **Use Controls \u0026 Docs Add-ons** for **dynamic component interaction**.  \n  \n✔ **Organize components by category** (&#96;Components/Button&#96; vs &#96;Components/Inputs&#96;).  \n  \n✔ **Automate visual \u0026 snapshot testing** to **catch unintended changes**.  \n  \n✔ **Deploy Storybook** as **live documentation** for developers \u0026 designers.  \n  \n✔ **Integrate Storybook in CI/CD** to ensure UI consistency. \n\n---\n\n## **Conclusion** \n\nStorybook is a **powerful tool for UI development, testing, and documentation**. It improves **component reusability, consistency, and collaboration** across teams. \n\n🚀 **Next Steps:**  \n  \n✅ Install Storybook and create your first component story.  \n  \n✅ Experiment with **Controls \u0026 Add-ons**.  \n  \n✅ Integrate Storybook into your **CI/CD pipeline**. \n\n---\n\n### **Tags** \n\nStorybook #Frontend #Testing #UIDevelopment #ComponentLibrary \n\n---\n\n###  TLDR – Highlights for Skimmers\n\n* Storybook isolates UI components for development and testing.\n* Controls allow dynamic prop changes inside Storybook UI.\n* Add-ons extend functionality (accessibility, documentation, testing).\n* Supports Jest, Testing Library, and Playwright for UI testing.\n* Mocks API responses with MSW for frontend testing.\n* Can be deployed as documentation on GitHub Pages or other platforms.\n\n---\n\n💬 **Have you used Storybook?** Share your experience in the comments!\n\n##  Top comments (1) \n\nSubscribe \n\npic \n\nPersonal Trusted User \n\n Create template \n\nTemplates let you quickly answer FAQs or store snippets for re-use.\n\nSubmit Preview Dismiss \n\nCollapse Expand \n\naustinwdigital profile image \n\nAustin Welsh \n\n Austin Welsh \n\n Austin Welsh \n\nFollow \n\n Senior Full Stack Developer @ Disney | JavaScript, TypeScript, React, Next.js\n\n* Location  \n United States\n* Work  \n Senior Full Stack Developer @ Disney\n* Joined  \nDec 21, 2024\n\n•  Feb 17 \n\nDropdown menu \n\n* Copy link\n* Hide\n\nWhat do you mainly use Storybook for?\n\nA) Component Development  \nB) UI Testing  \nC) Documentation  \nD) Something else\n\nLet me know!\n\nLike comment: Like comment: 1 like  Like Comment button Reply \n\n Some comments may only be visible to logged-in visitors. Conclusion\n\n# 1\\. Introduction to React Best Practices\n\nReact is a powerful JavaScript library for building interactive user interfaces. However, writing React code efficiently requires following best practices.\n\nBest practices help developers create applications that are easy to maintain, perform well, and provide a better user experience.\n\nIn this article, we will explore the most important best practices in React development to ensure your applications are optimized, secure, and scalable.\n\n# 2\\. Why Follow Best Practices in React?\n\nFollowing best practices in React ensures:\n\n* **Better Performance**: Optimized code leads to faster applications.\n* **Easy Maintainability**: Clean and structured code is easier to update.\n* **Scalability**: Applications can grow without performance issues.\n* **Fewer Bugs**: Adhering to best practices reduces errors.\n* **Improved User Experience**: Faster, smoother apps keep users engaged.\n\nNow, let’s dive into the essential best practices.\n\n# 3\\. Essential React Best Practices\n\n## 1\\. Use Functional Components Over Class Components\n\nFunctional components are preferred because they:\n\n* Require **less code** than class components.\n* Are **easier to read and maintain**.\n* Work well with **React Hooks** like useState and useEffect.\n\n## 2\\. Optimize Performance with React.memo and useCallback\n\n* **React.memo** helps prevent unnecessary re-renders of functional components.\n* **useCallback** ensures functions are not recreated unnecessarily, improving performance.\n\n## 3\\. Efficient State Management with React Context and Redux\n\n* Use **React Context API** for small applications where prop drilling becomes an issue.\n* Use **Redux** for larger applications that require centralized state management.\n\n## 4\\. Keep Components Small and Reusable\n\nBreaking components into **smaller, reusable pieces** makes the code:\n\n* **Easier to debug and maintain**.\n* **More readable and organized**.\n* **Reusable in multiple parts of the application**.\n\n## 5\\. Follow the DRY Principle (Don’t Repeat Yourself)\n\nAvoid writing duplicate code. Instead:\n\n* Use **reusable functions and components**.\n* Create **custom hooks** for repeating logic.\n* Keep styles and logic separate for better organization.\n\n## 6\\. Maintain Clean and Readable Code\n\nWrite code that is:\n\n* Well **formatted and commented**.\n* Follows **consistent naming conventions**.\n* Organized in a structured **folder hierarchy**.\n\n## 7\\. Leverage PropTypes and TypeScript for Type Safety\n\n* **PropTypes** help ensure correct prop types are passed to components.\n* **TypeScript** prevents runtime errors and improves code quality.\n\n## 8\\. Use Custom Hooks for Code Reusability\n\nIf multiple components use the same logic, extract it into a **custom hook** to make code cleaner and more reusable.\n\n## 9\\. Optimize Rendering with Key Attributes\n\nWhen rendering lists in React, always **use unique keys** to avoid unnecessary re-renders.\n\n## 10\\. Handle Side Effects Properly with useEffect\n\n* Always define **dependencies** inside useEffect to prevent infinite loops.\n* Use **cleanup functions** to avoid memory leaks.\n\n## 11\\. Implement Error Boundaries for Better Debugging\n\n* Use **Error Boundaries** to catch JavaScript errors in components.\n* Helps **prevent application crashes** by displaying fallback UI.\n\n## 12\\. Use Lazy Loading and Code Splitting\n\n* **React lazy** loads components only when needed, reducing initial load time.\n* **Code splitting** helps improve performance by loading only necessary code.\n\n# 4\\. Security Best Practices in React\n\n## 1\\. Prevent Cross-Site Scripting (XSS)\n\n* Always **sanitize user input** before rendering.\n* Avoid using **dangerouslySetInnerHTML** to prevent security vulnerabilities.\n\n## 2\\. Use Environment Variables for Sensitive Data\n\nStore API keys and private credentials in **environment variables** instead of hardcoding them in the code.\n\n## 3\\. Avoid Direct DOM Manipulation\n\nAlways use React’s **state and props** instead of directly modifying the DOM, as direct manipulation can lead to security issues.\n\n## 4\\. Keep Dependencies Updated\n\nRegularly **update npm packages** to fix security vulnerabilities and ensure the latest features and optimizations.\n\n# 5\\. SEO Best Practices for React Applications\n\n## 1\\. Implement Server-Side Rendering (SSR)\n\n* **Next.js** helps generate pages dynamically on the server, improving SEO.\n* Improves **search engine indexing and load time**.\n\n# 2\\. Use Static Site Generation (SSG) for Faster Performance\n\n* **SSG pre-builds pages**, making them load instantly.\n* Useful for pages that don’t change frequently, like blogs or product listings.\n\n# 3\\. Optimize Meta Tags and Structured Data\n\n* Use **React Helmet** to dynamically set meta tags like titles and descriptions.\n* Helps **search engines understand page content** better.\n\n# 4\\. Improve Page Load Speed\n\nTo improve speed:\n\n* Use **lazy loading** for images and components.\n* Minify and **bundle JavaScript and CSS**.\n* Enable **caching and compression techniques**.\n\n# 6\\. Conclusion\n\nFollowing best practices in React ensures your applications are:\n\n* **Fast** and high-performing.\n* **Secure** and less vulnerable to attacks.\n* **SEO-friendly** and discoverable by search engines.\n* **Maintainable** and easy to scale.\n\nBy implementing these best practices, developers can build React applications that are optimized, user-friendly, and future-proof.\n\nStay updated with the latest React updates to keep improving your development skills!\n\nReact\n\nReact Best Practices\n\nLazy Loading\n\nServer Side Rendering\n\nState Management\n\n\\--\n\n\\--\n\nReact Masters\n\nReact Masters\n\nWritten by React Masters\n\n209 followers\n\n·2 following\n\nReact Masters is one of the leading React JS training providers in Hyderabad. Report Abuse \n\nCover image for Building and Documenting UI Components with Storybook and React \n\nDebajit Mallick \n\nDebajit Mallick \n\n Posted on Mar 23 \n\n#  Building and Documenting UI Components with Storybook and React\n\n#react #storybook #frontend #documentation \n\n##  Introduction\n\nHave you ever struggled with maintaining consistency across your UI components or found it challenging to collaborate with designers? I've been there too. After experimenting with several tools, I discovered that Storybook changed my development workflow for the better.\n\nIn this post, I'll walk you through setting up Storybook in a React project and show you how to build and document components that you can reuse throughout your applications.\n\n##  What is Storybook?\n\nIt lets you build and test UI components in isolation, away from the complexity of the full app. The interactive documentation makes it easier for team members to understand how components work. Using Storybook, Setting up visual regression tests became surprisingly simple\n\n##  Getting Started: Project Setup\n\nLet's start by creating our project foundation. Fire up your terminal and run:  \n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\nnpm create vite@latest my-storybook-app -- --template react-ts\ncd my-storybook-app\nnpm install\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nEnter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode \n\nWith our React project ready, let's add Storybook to the mix:  \n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\nnpx storybook@latest init\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nEnter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode \n\nThis command works like magic – it automatically configures Storybook for your Vite setup, creates a &#96;.storybook/&#96; folder, and adds some example stories in &#96;src/stories/&#96;. Take a moment to explore these files to get familiar with the structure.\n\n##  Creating Our First Component: The Button\n\nLet's start by building a flexible Button component that we can reuse across our application.\n\nFirst, create the component file:  \n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n// src/components/Button.tsx\nimport React from 'react';\n\nexport interface ButtonProps {\n  label: string;\n  onClick?: () =\u003e void;\n  variant?: 'primary' | 'secondary';\n}\n\nexport const Button: React.FC\u003cButtonProps\u003e = ({\n  label,\n  onClick,\n  variant = 'primary',\n}) =\u003e {\n  const styles = {\n    primary: 'bg-blue-500 text-white',\n    secondary: 'bg-gray-200 text-black',\n  };\n\n  return (\n    \u003cbutton\n      className={&#96;px-4 py-2 rounded ${styles[variant]}&#96;}\n      onClick={onClick}\n    \u003e\n      {label}\n    \u003c/button\u003e\n  );\n};\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nEnter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode \n\nNow for the fun part – creating stories for our Button:  \n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n// src/components/Button.stories.tsx\nimport type { Meta, StoryObj } from '@storybook/react';\nimport { Button } from './Button';\n\nconst meta: Meta\u003ctypeof Button\u003e = {\n  title: 'Components/Button',\n  component: Button,\n};\n\nexport default meta;\ntype Story = StoryObj\u003ctypeof Button\u003e;\n\nexport const Primary: Story = {\n  args: {\n    label: 'Click Me',\n    variant: 'primary',\n  },\n};\n\nexport const Secondary: Story = {\n  args: {\n    label: 'Cancel',\n    variant: 'secondary',\n  },\n};\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nEnter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode \n\n##  Building a Card Component\n\nNow that we have our Button, let's create a Card component that can even incorporate our Button.  \n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n// src/components/Card.tsx\nimport React from 'react';\n\nexport interface CardProps {\n  title: string;\n  description: string;\n  children?: React.ReactNode;\n}\n\nexport const Card: React.FC\u003cCardProps\u003e = ({ title, description, children }) =\u003e {\n  return (\n    \u003cdiv className=\"border rounded-lg shadow-md p-4 max-w-sm\"\u003e\n      \u003ch3 className=\"text-lg font-bold mb-2\"\u003e{title}\u003c/h3\u003e\n      \u003cp className=\"text-gray-700 mb-4\"\u003e{description}\u003c/p\u003e\n      {children}\n    \u003c/div\u003e\n  );\n};\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nEnter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode \n\nAnd here's how we can showcase it in Storybook:  \n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n// src/components/Card.stories.tsx\nimport type { Meta, StoryObj } from '@storybook/react';\nimport { Card } from './Card';\nimport { Button } from './Button';\n\nconst meta: Meta\u003ctypeof Card\u003e = {\n  title: 'Components/Card',\n  component: Card,\n};\n\nexport default meta;\ntype Story = StoryObj\u003ctypeof Card\u003e;\n\nexport const Default: Story = {\n  args: {\n    title: 'Welcome!',\n    description: 'This is a sample card component.',\n  },\n};\n\nexport const WithButton: Story = {\n  render: (args) =\u003e (\n    \u003cCard {...args}\u003e\n      \u003cButton label=\"Learn More\" /\u003e\n    \u003c/Card\u003e\n  ),\n  args: {\n    title: 'Interactive Card',\n    description: 'This card includes a button as a child component.',\n  },\n};\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nEnter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode \n\nI particularly love this example because it shows how components can be nested in Storybook stories, helping you visualize complex component relationships.\n\n##  Adding Some Style with Tailwind (Optional)\n\nIf you're like me and prefer Tailwind for styling, it's super easy to add:  \n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\nnpm install -D tailwindcss postcss autoprefixer\nnpx tailwindcss init -p\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nEnter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode \n\nUpdate your CSS with:  \n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n/* in index.css */\n@tailwind base;\n@tailwind components;\n@tailwind utilities;\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nEnter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode \n\nDon't forget to add your source folder to the content paths in &#96;tailwind.config.js&#96;!\n\n##  Time to See It in Action!\n\nLet's fire up Storybook and see our components:  \n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\nnpm run storybook\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nEnter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode \n\nWhen you visit \u003chttp://localhost:6006/\u003e, you'll see your Button and Card components displayed in the Storybook UI. Try clicking around and interacting with different props – it's incredibly satisfying to see your components respond in real-time.\n\n##  Sharing Your Component Library\n\nWant to share your beautiful components with the team or showcase them in a portfolio? Generate a static build:  \n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\nnpm run build-storybook\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nEnter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode \n\nThis creates a &#96;storybook-static/&#96; directory that you can deploy to Netlify, Vercel, GitHub Pages, or any static hosting provider. I've found this especially useful when working with remote teams.\n\n##  Conclusion\n\nUsing Storybook you can develop a consistent design system. Which helps you to onboard new team members more quickly, catch UI bugs before they reach production. Also, you can Communicate more effectively with designers. If you like this blog and want to learn more about **Frontend Development** and **Software Engineering**, you can follow me on Dev.to.\n\n##  Top comments (0) \n\nSubscribe \n\npic \n\nPersonal Trusted User \n\n Create template \n\nTemplates let you quickly answer FAQs or store snippets for re-use.\n\nSubmit Preview Dismiss \n\nCode of Conduct • Report abuse \n\n Are you sure you want to hide this comment?       "chunk": "Sitemap\n\nOpen in app\n\nSign up\n\nSign in\n\nMedium Logo\n\nWrite\n\nSign up\n\nSign in\n\n# 10 Essential React.js Best Practices for Developers\n\nCodeaprogram\n\nCodeaprogram\n\n3 min read\n\n·\n\nJan 15, 2025\n\n\\--\n\nListen\n\nShare\n\nZoom image will be displayed\n\n# Introduction\n\nReact.js is one of the most popular JavaScript libraries for building user interfaces. As it evolves, so do the best practices for writing clean, maintainable, and efficient code. In this article, I’ll share 10 essential React.js best practices that every developer should follow in 2025.\n\n# 1\\. Use Functional Components Over Class Components\n\nFunctional components have become the standard in React development, especially with the introduction of hooks.\n\n* **Why?** They’re easier to read, test, and maintain.\n\nExample:\n\n// Functional Component  \nfunction Welcome({ name }) {  \n  return \u003ch1\u003eHello, {name}!\u003c/h1\u003e;  \n}\n\n# 2\\. Embrace React Hooks\n\nHooks like &#96;useState&#96;, &#96;useEffect&#96;, and &#96;useContext&#96; simplify state management and side effects in functional components.\n\n* Avoid overcomplicating with multiple &#96;useEffect&#96; calls in one component.\n* Example:\n\nimport { useState, useEffect } from 'react';  \n  \nfunction Counter() {  \n  const [count, setCount] = useState(0);  \n  \n  useEffect(() =\u003e {  \n    console.log(&#96;Count updated: ${count}&#96;);  \n  }, [count]);  \n  \n  return \u003cbutton onClick={() =\u003e setCount(count + 1)}\u003eCount: {count}\u003c/button\u003e;  \n}\n\n# 3\\. Structure Your Components Logically\n\nFollow a consistent folder structure to keep your project organized.\n\n* Example:\n\nsrc/  \n  components/  \n    Button/  \n      Button.jsx  \n      Button.css  \n    Header/  \n      Header.jsx  \n      Header.css  \n  hooks/  \n    useFetch.js  \n  utils/  \n    formatDate.js\n\n# 4\\. Use PropTypes or TypeScript\n\nValidate props to make your components more robust.\n\n* **Using PropTypes:**\n\nimport PropTypes from 'prop-types';  \n  \nfunction Button({ label }) {  \n  return \u003cbutton\u003e{label}\u003c/button\u003e;  \n}  \n  \nButton.propTypes = {  \n  label: PropTypes.string.isRequired,  \n};\n\n* **Using TypeScript:**\n\ntype ButtonProps = {  \n  label: string;  \n};  \n  \nconst Button: React.FC\u003cButtonProps\u003e = ({ label }) =\u003e {  \n  return \u003cbutton\u003e{label}\u003c/button\u003e;  \n};\n\n# 5\\. Optimize React Performance\n\n* Use &#96;React.memo&#96; to prevent unnecessary re-renders.\n* Avoid anonymous functions in props.\n* Example with &#96;React.memo&#96;:\n\nconst Greeting = React.memo(({ name }) =\u003e {  \n  console.log('Rendering Greeting');  \n  return \u003ch1\u003eHello, {name}!\u003c/h1\u003e;  \n});\n\n# 6\\. Use Context API for State Management\n\nFor small to medium applications, avoid heavy libraries like Redux unless necessary.\n\nimport { createContext, useContext } from 'react';  \n  \nconst ThemeContext = createContext('light');  \n  \nfunction ThemeProvider({ children }) {  \n  const theme = 'dark';  \n  return (  \n    \u003cThemeContext.Provider value={theme}\u003e  \n      {children}  \n    \u003c/ThemeContext.Provider\u003e  \n  );  \n}  \n  \nfunction App() {  \n  const theme = useContext(ThemeContext);  \n  return \u003cdiv className={&#96;theme-${theme}&#96;}\u003eCurrent Theme: {theme}\u003c/div\u003e;  \n}\n\n# 7\\. Code Splitting and Lazy Loading\n\nUse dynamic imports to split code and improve performance.\n\nimport React, { Suspense } from 'react';  \nconst LazyComponent = React.lazy(() =\u003e import('./LazyComponent'));  \n  \nfunction App() {  \n  return (  \n    \u003cSuspense fallback={\u003cdiv\u003eLoading...\u003c/div\u003e}\u003e  \n      \u003cLazyComponent /\u003e  \n    \u003c/Suspense\u003e  \n  );  \n}\n\n# 8\\. Avoid Inline Styles for Complex UI\n\nUse CSS modules or styled-components for better maintainability.\n\n* **Using CSS Modules:**\n\nimport styles from './Button.module.css';  \n  \nfunction Button() {  \n  return \u003cbutton className={styles.primary}\u003eClick Me\u003c/button\u003e;  \n}\n\n# 9\\. Write Reusable Components\n\nBuild components that are generic and customizable.\n\nfunction Input({ type = 'text', placeholder }) {  \n  return \u003cinput type={type} placeholder={placeholder} /\u003e;  \n}\n\n# 10\\.
